# Closing the loop: Ashby's ultrastable system and why today's AI systems disappoint

*Ultrastable white paper. Ultrastable is the foundation for any autonomous system.*

## Abstract

W. Ross Ashby (John Wiley & Sons, New York): An adaptive system keeps its essential variables within limits through two feedbacks: a first loop that reacts to the environment, and a second loop that changes the first loop's parameters (step-functions) only when an essential variable leaves its limits, and keeps changing them until a configuration holds the variables in bounds. Ultrastable takes its name from Ashby's ultrastable system. Most current AI systems answer and stop: nothing checks the result against limits and changes the system when it fails, so their loops stay open. We state Ashby's mechanism as a set of testable properties, check each against this system's code and records, and show where the code falls short. 4 of 5 are met today; each one that is not is an open work item with a closing probe, and this paper is regenerated from the measurements after every merge.

## 1. Introduction

A common view holds that AI systems are smart enough already; what holds them back is model capability. This paper tests a different account: what holds most AI systems back is an open loop: nothing checks the result against limits and changes the system when it fails. That is an engineering property, and it can be tested.

Ultrastable takes its name from Ashby's ultrastable system. Most current AI systems answer and stop: nothing checks the result against limits and changes the system when it fails, so their loops stay open. We state Ashby's mechanism as a set of testable properties, check each against this system's code and records, and show where the code falls short.

The question is narrow and testable. For each of 5 findings we name the concern, the mechanism in this system that is meant to answer it, and a metric from the system's own records that can show the answer does not hold. The findings cover oversight, reliability, systems.

Metrics come from the system's own files: ops/research/prs.json (closed pull requests read from GitHub), ops/deploys.jsonl, ops/criticality.jsonl, ops/ultrastability.jsonl, doctrine/ultrastability.json, the loop registry and git history. Each finding is stated as a target on one metric, with a prediction logged before the measurement. A finding is met only when the measured value meets the target; a metric with no readings is reported as not measured, never as met.

## 5. Discussion

A1. An essential variable without limits. In Ashby's account, adaptation is defined by keeping certain essential variables within limits. A variable with no limits can never trigger the second loop, so a system that declares one without limits is not ultrastable in that variable. [1] In this system the answer is ULTRASTABILITY-1 (every essential variable is declared with its limits, per scope (platform, tenant)); ASHBY-1 (the check fails when an essential variable has neither a lower nor an upper limit). The metric, share of declared essential variables that have limits (doctrine/ultrastability.json), reads 1.0 (n = 13) against a target of >= 1.0. The mechanism holds on this evidence.

A2. A second loop that never acts. The second feedback runs through the essential variables: when one leaves its limits, the system changes itself. A second loop that is declared but never steps is a diagram, not a mechanism. [1] In this system the answer is ULTRASTABILITY-1 (after patience_ticks readings out of limits, one step is taken and logged with a prediction); CLOCKWORK-1 (the second loop runs on the watchdog clock and on the cost guard, server-side). The metric, second-order steps the ultrastability loop took in the last 30 days (ops/ultrastability.jsonl), reads 98 (n = 13990) against a target of >= 1. The mechanism holds on this evidence.

A3. Nothing the second loop can change. Ashby's preface: "any system which shows adaptation must (1) contain many variables that behave as step-functions". The second loop changes the first loop's parameters; where it can only file a work item, the change waits on another loop. [1] In this system the answer is ULTRASTABILITY-1 (a ladder step of kind param changes a declared value the first loop reads, inside declared limits). The metric, share of essential variables whose second loop can change a parameter of the first loop, reads 1.0 (n = 13) against a target of >= 0.5. The mechanism holds on this evidence.

A4. A search that stops before anything holds. The ultrastable system keeps changing its step-functions until it reaches a configuration that holds the essential variables within limits, and then keeps it. A loop that gives up after a fixed list of tries, or never finds a configuration that holds, has not adapted. [1] In this system the answer is ASHBY-SEARCH-1 (after the ladder, untried parameter values are drawn until one holds or the declared range is spent; only then a redesign item); ULTRASTABILITY-1 (a step is kept only when the variable is back inside its limits within settle_ticks; otherwise it is undone). The metric, share of second-order steps that brought the variable back inside its limits and were kept, reads 0.0 (n = 91) against a target of >= 0.25. The mechanism does not yet hold; work item Q-RES-ashby-1952-A4 carries the fix and closes only when the same measurement passes.

A5. AI systems leave their loops open. Ultrastable's reading, not Ashby's words: a chat model or coding agent produces an answer and stops. Nothing checks the result against limits and changes the system when it fails, so the loop is open, and disappointment follows. Every loop Ultrastable runs is meant to carry its own closing check. [1] In this system the answer is CLOSED-LOOP-1 (an output with no code consumer fails the build); SERVER-OWNS-LOOPS-1 (every loop has a server-side owner; a client session never closes one). The metric, share of registered loops that declare a closing probe and a server-side owner, reads 1.0 (n = 112) against a target of >= 1.0. The mechanism holds on this evidence.

## 6. Limitations

- Reading. Chapters 7 and 8 were not machine-read for this paper: the archive.org text the research loop could reach ends in chapter 2. Ashby's mechanism is stated here in our own words from the book's contents and preface; the only verbatim quotation is from the preface (page v).
- Search. Ashby's step-functions take new values at random. Ultrastable first takes a fixed ladder of steps, then draws untried values at random (seeded, so a run can be replayed) from each parameter's declared range. A restructure step is a work item for the executor, not a step-function, and depends on the executor completing it.
- Declared versus observed. The closed-loop share counts loops that declare a closing probe and a server-side owner; it does not show that each probe passes today.
- Source. Book, version 1952, reprinted with corrections 1954.

## 7. Conclusion

On this system's records, 4 of 5 findings hold. The gaps are a search that stops before anything holds.

That is evidence against the view that AI is held back by model capability: the properties tested here are engineering properties of the loop, and each can be measured and repaired without waiting on a better model.

The paper is regenerated from the measurements after every merge, so a reader who returns later sees the current result, not this one.
